subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
description: Students read and comprehend grade-appropriate literary nonfiction and informational texts within the grades 6 to 8 text complexity band and demonstrate understanding by answering questions about them. They locate information stated explicitly, determine the meaning of unfamiliar academic and content words from context, track the central idea and the supporting details that develop it, follow how ideas, events, or steps are organized and connected, distinguish facts from the author's opinions or claims, and draw reasonable inferences and conclusions supported by evidence in the text. This is an integrative comprehension skill: rather than isolating one strategy, each item asks the student to make sense of a complete nonfiction excerpt (such as a biography, history account, science explanation, essay, or news report) at a level of complexity appropriate to sixth grade. Every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Locate and comprehend information stated explicitly in an informational passage
Determine the meaning of unfamiliar academic, technical, or content-area words using context clues in the passage
Identify the central idea of a passage and distinguish it from the supporting details
Follow how a text is organized (chronological, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, or sequence of steps) and how ideas connect
Distinguish statements of fact from the author's opinions, claims, or point of view
Draw reasonable inferences and conclusions that are supported by evidence in the text
Summarize an informational passage objectively without copying it word for word and without adding personal opinion
Sustain comprehension across a longer, denser, or more technical passage at the upper end of the grade band

problemArchetypes.name: Comprehend explicit detail
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'Honeybees communicate the location of food through movement. When a scout returns to the hive, it performs a looping dance. The angle of the dance points other bees toward the flowers, and the length of the dance tells them how far to fly.' Question: According to the passage, what does the length of a honeybee's dance tell the other bees? Answer: How far they must fly to reach the flowers, because the text states this directly.

problemArchetypes.name: Determine word meaning from context
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'The desert tortoise is well adapted to drought. It can store water in its bladder for months and slow its body down during the driest part of the year, surviving long stretches with almost no rain.' Question: What does the word 'drought' mean as it is used here? Answer: A long period with very little or no rain, because the passage describes surviving months with almost no rain.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify central idea and supporting detail
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'Recycling one aluminum can saves enough energy to power a television for three hours. Aluminum can be melted down and reused again and again without losing quality. Unlike paper, it does not break down in landfills for hundreds of years. For these reasons, recycling aluminum is one of the most effective things a household can do.' Question: Which sentence best states the central idea of the passage? Answer: Recycling aluminum is an especially effective action because the metal saves energy, can be reused endlessly, and does not break down in landfills.

problemArchetypes.name: Analyze text structure and connections
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'In 1845, an explorer led two ships into the Arctic to find a northern sea route. The ships became trapped in ice and never returned. Searchers spent the next decade looking for them. It was not until 2014 that one of the wrecks was finally located on the ocean floor.' Question: How are the ideas in this passage mainly organized? Answer: In chronological order, because the passage moves through events from 1845 to 2014 in the order they happened.

problemArchetypes.name: Distinguish fact from opinion or claim
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'The new city library is open seven days a week and holds more than forty thousand books. In my view, it is the finest building in the entire town, and everyone should visit it at least once a month.' Question: Which statement from the passage is an opinion rather than a fact? Answer: That the library is the finest building in town, because it expresses a personal judgment that cannot be checked, unlike the hours and the number of books.

problemArchetypes.name: Draw an evidence-based inference or conclusion
problemArchetypes.example: Passage: 'For weeks the scientists had seen no sign of the rare frog. Then, after the first heavy rains of the season, the pond filled and the night air filled with croaking. By morning the team had recorded dozens of the frogs along the water's edge.' Question: What can the reader most reasonably conclude about the frogs? Answer: The frogs become active and gather after heavy rain fills the pond, because they appeared in large numbers only once the rains came, even though the passage never states this rule outright.

Easy.description: A short informational stimulus of roughly 3 to 5 sentences (about 40 to 75 words) at the lower edge of the grade band, embedded in the item, on a concrete and familiar topic. The question targets information stated explicitly or a single clear context clue, and the answer can be located almost directly in the text. Vocabulary is mostly everyday with at most one supported content word. Minimal inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is 3 to 5 sentences (about 40 to 75 words) included in the prompt
Topic is concrete and familiar (a simple science fact, a short how-to, a brief biography fact)
Targets an explicit detail or one clearly signaled context-clue word
Identify-level task: locate the answer that the passage states or signals directly
Distractors are real details from elsewhere in the passage or plainly off topic

Medium.description: An informational stimulus of roughly 6 to 10 sentences (about 90 to 140 words), such as a full nonfiction paragraph or a short two-paragraph explanation, embedded in the item. The task requires a single-step inference, identifying the central idea versus a supporting detail, recognizing the text's organizational structure, distinguishing a fact from an opinion or claim, or determining a less obvious academic or content word from context. The student must connect details rather than copy one sentence, and distractors are real text details that are too narrow, partial, or off point.
constraints: Stimulus is a 6 to 10 sentence passage or short two-paragraph explanation in the prompt
Topic may be less familiar (history, science process, current events, an essay claim)
Targets a one-step inference, a central-idea or summary judgment, a text-structure identification, or a fact-versus-opinion distinction
Analyze-level task: combine two or more details to reach a supported conclusion
Distractors are genuine but weaker readings, partial summaries, or surface-only details

Hard.description: A richer informational stimulus of roughly 11 to 16 sentences (about 160 to 240 words) at the upper end of the grades 6 to 8 band, with denser content, more academic or technical vocabulary, and more implicit or layered ideas, embedded in the item. The task requires multi-step inference or evaluation: judging the best objective summary of a developing explanation, inferring an author's point of view or purpose, synthesizing several details into the central idea, analyzing how one section builds on another, or interpreting a content word in a precise context. The student must hold the whole passage in mind and weigh competing reasonable-sounding options.
constraints: Stimulus is an 11 to 16 sentence passage or short multi-paragraph article in the prompt
Topic is academic or technical (a science mechanism, a historical cause-and-effect account, a persuasive essay)
Targets multi-step inference about central idea, author's purpose or point of view, or how ideas develop across the passage
Evaluate-level task: select the best overall objective summary or interpretation and reject close-but-wrong ones
Distractors include a true-but-too-narrow detail, an overstated or off-topic reading, an opinion mistaken for the main idea, and a conclusion that goes beyond the evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a reasonable-sounding outside assumption as if the passage said it, answering from prior knowledge rather than the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a fact or conclusion that fits what the student already believes about the topic but is never stated or supported in the passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a small supporting detail with the central idea and summarizes only one part of the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a summary that restates a single vivid statistic or example rather than the main point the whole passage develops

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student cannot tell the author's opinion or claim apart from a checkable fact
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a value judgment such as 'it is the finest building in town' as a fact, or labels a verifiable statistic as an opinion

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student guesses a content or academic word's meaning from how it looks or sounds instead of using the context clues in the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Defines 'drought' as 'a kind of plant' because it resembles a familiar word, ignoring the surrounding description of months with almost no rain

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misreads the text's organization and so reverses or scrambles the relationship among ideas or events
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Treats a chronological account as cause and effect, or claims an effect came before its cause, contradicting the order the passage gives

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses an inference with something stated explicitly, treating a reader conclusion as a direct statement in the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Marks 'the frogs come out after heavy rain' as directly stated when the passage only describes one event from which the pattern must be inferred

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student draws a conclusion that goes beyond what the evidence in the passage can support
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes that recycling aluminum solves all pollution when the passage only claims it is one effective household action

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds personal opinion or judgment into what should be an objective summary of an informational text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a summary that inserts the reader's own view ('this is the best idea') instead of neutrally restating the passage's main point
